[[_update-email-workflow]]

== Update Email Workflow (UpdateEmail)

With this workflow, users will have to use an `UPDATE_EMAIL` action to change their own email address.

This action provides a more secure and consistent flow to update user emails by requiring re-authentication and optionally requiring email verification before any update to their account.

Applications are able to send their users to the email update form by leveraging UPDATE_EMAIL as an <<con-aia_{context},AIA (Application Initiated Action)>>.

To enable Update Email capability for a realm, go to the `Authentication` menu in the administration console and click on `Required actions` tab.
Switch the toggle for `UPDATE_EMAIL` required action to `enabled`.

=== Forcing users to re-authenticate before updating email

When the `UPDATE_EMAIL` required action is enabled, users may be required to re-authenticate before being able to update their email if their last authentication is older than the configured duration.
This is a security measure to prevent account takeover in case the user credentials are not known by the attacker but the user session is hijacked.

By default, the user will be asked to re-authenticate if the last authentication is older than 5 minutes (300 seconds). You
can change this value by setting the `Maximum Age of Authentication` setting in the `UPDATE_EMAIL` required action configuration.
By setting this value to `0`, the user will always be asked to re-authenticate before updating the email.

=== Verifying Emails

If the realm has email verification disabled, this action will allow to update the email without verification.

If the realm has email verification enabled, the action will send an email with a link to the new email address without changing the account email.
Only after following the link and confirming the email, the email will be updated.

Under certain circumstances, you do not want to enable email verification at the realm level but only when users are updating their emails.
For that, you can set the `Force Email Verification` setting on the `UPDATE_EMAIL` required action to force users to verify their emails
even though email verification is eventually disabled at the realm level. By default, email verification is not enabled.

In case the user is updating the email during the authentication flow (e.g.: when running the `UPDATE_PROFILE` required action),
the user will be forced to verify the email if any of the `Verify Email` or the `Force Email Verification` settings are enabled.
In case the `Verify Email` is enabled at the realm level, the `VERIFY_EMAIL` required action will be automatically added to the user account.
Otherwise, if only the `Force Email Verification` is enabled the `UPDATE_EMAIL` required
action will be added instead.

If a user has `Email Verified` set, and both `Verify Email` and `Force Email Verification` are disabled, `Email Verified`
resets after the user updates email.

=== Updating the user email

When the `UPDATE_EMAIL` required action is enabled, the user can update their emails by:

* Self-registering to a realm if this capability is enabled to realm
* Accessing the account console and clicking the `Update email` link when at the `Personal info` section
* Updating the profile during the authentication flow (e.g.: when running the `UPDATE_PROFILE` required action) if the email is not yet set.
If an existing user does have an email set when updating the profile during the authentication flow, the email attribute will not be available.
* Administrators when updating the user account through the administration console

=== Pending Email Verification

When a user initiates an email update that requires verification, the new email address is stored in a pending state until the user clicks the verification link. If the user tries to log in again before clicking the verification link, they will see a message informing them that a verification email was sent to the new address, with options to resend the email or enter a different email address.

Administrators can manage these pending verifications through the admin console. In the user details page, when a user has a pending email verification, a warning alert is displayed indicating the pending verification status. The alert shows which email address is awaiting confirmation and provides a link to cancel the verification process.

Clicking this link opens a confirmation dialog that allows administrators to remove the pending verification or cancel the action.

When confirmed, this action will:

* Remove the pending email verification attribute
* Invalidate the existing verification link  
* Remove the `UPDATE_EMAIL` required action from the user

=== Update Email and User Profile

If the email attribute is set as required in the user profile configuration, the requirement is kept in the Update Email workflow,
meaning a user won't be able to clear his/her email in update email page. The opposite is true, if the email attribute is set as optional
in the user profile configuration.

If the email attribute is set as read-only in the user profile configuration, the following behavior applies:

* The `Update email` link will not be displayed in the account console
* The `UPDATE_EMAIL` required action will be automatically skipped and removed from the user account
* In the update profile page, if the user's email is initially empty, the email field will be hidden

=== Message Customization

All messages displayed in this workflow, including admin console messages, verification emails, and update email page messages, can be customized using the standard {project_name} message customization system.

[[_oid4vci_credential_offer_aia]]
=== Credential Offer via Application Initiated Action

{project_name} provides a built-in <<con-aia_{context},Application Initiated Action (AIA)>> called `verifiable_credential_offer` that allows client applications to trigger credential issuance for a user during login. When this action is triggered, the user is presented with a page containing a QR code that can be scanned by a wallet application to claim the credential.

Both the {project_name} <<_account-service,Account Console>> (*Verifiable credentials* tab → *Issue to wallet*) and the Admin Console (*Users* → *Verifiable Credentials* → *Send credential offer*) use this same AIA under the covers.

This section covers how to configure the action, how to trigger it from your application, and what the user experiences during the flow.

==== Enabling and configuring the action

The `verifiable_credential_offer` action is automatically registered when the `OID4VC_VCI` feature is enabled. You can manage it in the Admin Console:

. Navigate to *Authentication* > *Required actions*.
. Locate the *Register Verifiable Credential Offer* action in the list.

.Required Actions configuration showing the Verifiable Credential Offer action
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-required-actions-vc-offer.png[Required Actions tab showing the Register Verifiable Credential Offer action with its enabled toggle and re-auth max age setting, width=750]

From here you can:

* **Disable the action** — Toggle it off to prevent any application from triggering credential offers via AIA.
* **Configure re-authentication** — Set the *Max Age* to control how long ago the user must have actively authenticated before being required to re-authenticate when the action is triggered. Set it to `0` to always require active re-authentication. If not configured, the default is five minutes. See <<con-aia-reauth_{context},Re-authentication during AIA>> for details.

==== Triggering the action from your application

To trigger the credential offer AIA, your application redirects the user to the {project_name} authorization endpoint with the `kc_action` parameter. The parameter value consists of the action name followed by a colon and a Base64Url-encoded JSON configuration:

[source]
----
kc_action=verifiable_credential_offer:<base64url-encoded-config>
----

The JSON configuration object has the following properties:

[cols="1,1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Property
| Required
| Description

| `credentialConfigurationId`
| Yes
| The type of credential to offer. This value must match the *Credential Configuration ID* attribute of an existing OID4VCI client scope (see <<_oid4vci_client_scope,Create Client Scopes with Mappers>>), and the authenticated user must already have this credential assigned (see <<_oid4vci_user_setup,Creating a User Account>>). If the user does not have the credential, the AIA returns `kc_action_status=error`. It identifies a credential _type_ (such as "membership-credential" or "employee-badge"), not a specific issued credential. This is the same identifier that appears in the issuer metadata under `credential_configurations_supported`.

| `preAuthorized`
| No
| If `true`, the credential offer uses the pre-authorized code grant, which requires the `oid4vc-vci-preauth-code` feature to be enabled (`--features=oid4vc-vci-preauth-code`). If `false` or omitted, the authorization code grant is used.

| `clientId`
| No
| The client ID of the OID4VCI-enabled client to which this offer is restricted. This is the human-readable client ID (for example, `my-wallet-client`), not Keycloak's internal UUID. The specified client must be enabled and have OID4VCI turned on. If omitted, the credential offer can be used by any client or wallet.
|===

===== Example

To trigger a credential offer for a credential configuration called `membership-credential` using the authorization code grant:

. Construct the JSON configuration:
+
[source,json]
----
{"credentialConfigurationId":"membership-credential"}
----

. Base64Url-encode the JSON string. For example, the above encodes to:
+
[source]
----
eyJjcmVkZW50aWFsQ29uZmlndXJhdGlvbklkIjoibWVtYmVyc2hpcC1jcmVkZW50aWFsIn0
----

. Append it to the `kc_action` parameter and redirect the user to the authorization endpoint:
+
[source,http]
----
GET /realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/auth
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=my-app
  &redirect_uri=https://my-app.example.com/callback
  &scope=openid
  &kc_action=verifiable_credential_offer:eyJjcmVkZW50aWFsQ29uZmlndXJhdGlvbklkIjoibWVtYmVyc2hpcC1jcmVkZW50aWFsIn0
----

===== Handling the response

After the user completes or cancels the action, they are redirected back to your application's redirect URI. The redirect includes:

* `kc_action_status=success` — The user completed the credential offer flow.
* `kc_action_status=cancelled` — The user cancelled the action.

[source]
----
https://my-app.example.com/callback?code=...&kc_action_status=success&kc_action=verifiable_credential_offer
----

[WARNING]
====
Even if `kc_action_status=success` is returned, this only means the user completed the AIA flow — it does not guarantee the wallet successfully obtained the credential. On the contrary, when the AIA was cancelled, it is still possible that wallet successfully obtained the credential. The credential is issued asynchronously when the wallet contacts {project_name}'s credential endpoint.
====

==== The credential offer QR code page

When the AIA is triggered and the user has authenticated (or re-authenticated if required), {project_name} displays a credential offer page. This page presents two ways for the user to claim the credential:

* **QR code** — The user scans the QR code with a wallet application on another device. The QR code encodes an `openid-credential-offer://` URI that the wallet uses to retrieve the credential offer from {project_name}.
* **Offer URL link** — For same-device wallets, the user can click the link directly to open the offer in a wallet application installed on the same device.

.Credential offer page with QR code
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-aia-credential-offer-qr.png[Credential offer page showing a QR code and an Offer URL link for claiming a verifiable credential, width=650]

The page displays two steps to guide the user:

. Scan the QR code or click the offer URL to claim the credential with a wallet.
. Click *Continue* to proceed with login after the credential has been obtained.

The user can also click *Cancel* to abort the credential offer and return to the application. When the action is admin-initiated (triggered via email link), the cancel button is hidden.

==== Sending a credential offer from the Admin Console

Administrators can send a credential offer to a user by email directly from the Admin Console. This is useful when the administrator wants to proactively issue a credential to a user without requiring the user to initiate the flow from a client application.

===== Prerequisites

* The user must have an email address configured.
* SMTP must be configured for the realm (see <<_email,Configuring email for a realm>>).
* The user must have at least one verifiable credential assigned (see <<_oid4vci_user_setup,Creating a User Account>>).

===== Sending the offer

. In the Admin Console, navigate to *Users* and select the target user.
. Switch to the *Verifiable Credentials* tab. This tab lists the verifiable credentials available to the user.
+
.User Verifiable Credentials tab in the Admin Console
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-user-verifiable-credentials-tab.png[Admin Console showing the Verifiable Credentials tab for a user with a list of available credentials and a Send credential offer action, width=750]

. Click *Send credential offer* for the credential you want to issue.
. In the dialog that appears, configure the offer lifespan — this determines how long the email link remains valid.
+
.Send credential offer dialog
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-send-credential-offer-dialog.png[Send credential offer dialog showing a lifespan selector for configuring how long the email link remains valid, width=500]

. Click *Send* to deliver the email.

The user receives an email containing a link. When the user clicks the link, they are first shown a confirmation page asking them to confirm they want to claim the credential. After they click the proceed link, they are taken to the credential offer QR code page described above, where they can scan the QR code or click the offer URL to claim the credential with their wallet. Since this is an admin-initiated action, the cancel button is not shown on the credential offer page.

[NOTE]
====
The email link uses {project_name}'s action token mechanism. The lifespan of the link is configurable in the dialog and defaults to the realm's *Default Admin-Initiated Action Lifespan* setting, which is 12 hours by default. If the link expires before the user clicks it, they will see an error page.
====

[[_oid4vci_managing_credentials]]
=== Managing Issued Credentials

Before issuing credentials, administrators must configure an OID4VCI client scope and assign a verifiable credential to the user (see <<_oid4vci_user_setup, Creating a User Account>>). Once issued via the OID4VCI protocol, credentials can be viewed, managed, and revoked by administrators through the Admin Console or Admin REST API, or by users through the Account Console. This section explains how to manage the credential lifecycle and handle compromise scenarios.

==== Viewing Credential Entitlements

A credential entitlement represents a user's authorization to receive a specific type of Verifiable Credential. Administrators assign these entitlements before credentials can be issued.

To view a user's credential entitlements:

. In the Admin Console, click *Users* in the menu.
. Select the user.
. Click the *Verifiable Credentials* tab.

.Verifiable Credentials tab showing credential entitlements
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-user-vc-tab.png[Verifiable Credentials tab on the user detail page, width=750]

The table lists each credential type assigned to the user. Use the kebab menu on each row to access available actions.

.Available actions for a credential entitlement
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-user-verifiable-credentials-tab.png[Kebab menu showing available actions for a credential entitlement, width=750]

The following actions are available:

* *View Attributes* -- Shows the user attribute snapshot associated with this credential type.
* *View Issued Credentials* -- Opens a detail view of all credentials issued to the user for this type.
* *Update Credential* -- Refreshes the stored user attributes and increments the credential revision.
* *Revoke* -- Removes the credential entitlement and deletes all issued credential records for that user and credential type.
* *Send Credential Offer* -- Sends a credential offer to the user via email (requires the user to have an email address configured).

[[_oid4vci_attribute_snapshot]]
==== Understanding Attribute Snapshots and Credential Claims

When an administrator creates a verifiable credential entitlement for a user, {project_name} stores a snapshot of the user's attributes with the entitlement. The *Update Credential* action refreshes the stored snapshot and increments the credential revision.

The stored snapshot is not used to populate credential claims. When {project_name} issues or refreshes a credential, protocol mappers configured on the OID4VCI client scope read the user's current attributes. The snapshot does not freeze the values of claims mapped from user attributes.

The consequences are:

* If a mapped user attribute, such as the family name, changes after the administrator grants the credential, the next issued or refreshed credential contains the current attribute value. This change does not require a credential update or renewed administrator approval.
* Existing refresh tokens remain valid after a credential update changes the revision. The wallet can continue to refresh the credential, and claims mapped from user attributes contain the current values.

This behavior is permitted by
https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-credential-issuance-1_0.html#multiple-accesses-to-the-credential-endpoint[Section 14.3 of the OID4VCI specification] and
https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-credential-issuance-1_0.html#refreshing-issued-credentials[Section 14.5 of the OID4VCI specification].
The specification allows the issuer to return either the same or updated claim values in subsequent credentials.

[NOTE]
====
Future releases might support issuance from the administrator-approved attribute snapshot and refresh token revocation when a credential is updated.
====

==== Viewing Issued Credentials

Each credential entitlement can have multiple issued credential records -- for example, when the credential is issued through independent authorization grants or wallet clients. Refreshing through an existing refresh token reuses its issued credential record.

To view individual issued credentials:

. Navigate to *Users* > select the user > *Verifiable Credentials* tab.
. Click the kebab menu on a credential entitlement row.
. Select *View Issued Credentials*.

.Issued credentials detail view
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-user-issued-credentials-detail.png[Individual issued credentials showing id and issuedAt and expiresAt and walletClient and revision, width=750]

Each issued credential shows:

* *ID* -- The unique identifier of the issued credential record.
* *Issued At* -- When the credential was issued.
* *Expires At* -- When the credential record expires (based on the *Credential Lifetime* setting of the OID4VCI client scope).
* *Wallet Client* -- The OID4VCI client through which the credential was issued.
* *Revision* -- The credential revision number. An "outdated" label appears if the credential was issued with an older revision of the stored attribute snapshot. The revision does not determine the values of claims mapped from user attributes. For details, see <<_oid4vci_attribute_snapshot,Understanding Attribute Snapshots and Credential Claims>>.

==== Credential Revocation

===== Understanding Revocation in OID4VCI

{project_name} uses a two-tier revocation model for Verifiable Credentials:

* *Revoking an individual issued credential* -- Removes the specific credential record from the database. The wallet can no longer refresh this credential.
* *Revoking a credential type entitlement* -- Removes the user's authorization for that credential type and deletes all issued credential records for that user and type, preventing future issuance.

[IMPORTANT]
====
Revocation on the server side removes the database record and prevents future credential refresh. However, a Verifiable Credential already held by a wallet remains cryptographically valid until its `exp` (expiration) claim passes. There is currently no status list mechanism for verifiers to check whether a credential has been revoked on the server. To limit exposure from compromised credentials, configure a short *Credential Refresh Interval* (`vc.refresh_interval_in_seconds`).
====

===== Revoking Individual Issued Credentials

To revoke a specific issued credential through the Admin Console:

. Navigate to *Users* > select the user > *Verifiable Credentials* tab.
. Click the kebab menu on the credential entitlement row and select *View Issued Credentials*.
. Click *Revoke* on the specific issued credential.
. Confirm the revocation in the confirmation dialog.

.Revoking an individual issued credential
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-user-issued-credential-revoke-confirm.png[Confirmation dialog when revoking an individual issued credential, width=650]

Using the Admin REST API:

[source,bash]
----
DELETE /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{userId}/vc/issued-credentials/{credentialId}
----

===== Revoking Credential Type Entitlements

Revoking a credential type entitlement removes the entitlement and *also deletes all issued credential records* for that user and credential type. This is a destructive operation that cannot be undone.

To revoke a user's entitlement to a credential type:

. Navigate to *Users* > select the user > *Verifiable Credentials* tab.
. Click the kebab menu on the credential entitlement row and select *Revoke*.
. Confirm the revocation.

.Revoking a credential type entitlement
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-user-vc-entitlement-revoke-confirm.png[Confirmation dialog when revoking a credential type entitlement, width=650]

Using the Admin REST API:

[source,bash]
----
DELETE /admin/realms/{realm}/users/{userId}/vc/credentials/{scopeName}
----

==== Refresh Token and Credential Lifecycle

The OID4VCI credential lifecycle is governed by two time-based settings configured on the OID4VCI client scope:

* *Credential Lifetime* -- How long the credential record and its refresh token remain valid. Default *365 days* (31536000 seconds).
* *Credential Refresh Interval* -- How often the wallet must refresh the credential. This value sets the `exp` (expiration) claim in the issued VC JWT. Default *7 days* (604800 seconds), or the credential lifetime if shorter.

.Credential Lifetime and Refresh Interval settings on the OID4VCI client scope
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-oid4vci-scope-lifetime-settings.png[OID4VCI client scope configuration showing Credential Lifetime and Credential Refresh Interval fields, width=750]

With the default settings, the credential refresh cycle works as follows:

. *Day 0* -- Wallet receives a credential (expires in 7 days) and a refresh token (expires in 365 days)
. *Day 7* -- The credential in the wallet is expired. The wallet automatically uses its refresh token to obtain a new access token from the token endpoint, then calls the credential endpoint to receive a freshly signed credential (expires Day 14).
. *Day 14, 21, 28...* -- The same refresh cycle repeats automatically. The user is never prompted to re-authenticate.
. *Day 365* -- The refresh token expires. The user must re-authenticate to obtain a new credential.

This design ensures the wallet always holds a recently signed credential (limiting exposure if a credential is compromised), while the user only needs to log in once per credential lifetime.

The credential lifecycle is also affected by the following events:

* *Refresh token revocation* -- When a wallet explicitly revokes a refresh token through the token revocation endpoint, {project_name} removes the corresponding issued credential record from the database. Ordinary user logout or removal of an individual session does not affect the refresh token or the issued credential record, since OID4VCI refresh tokens are session-independent. Setting the user's not-before policy (for example, through *Sign out all active sessions*) prevents further refresh but leaves the issued credential record stored as stale.
* *Credential entitlement revocation* -- When an administrator or user revokes the credential type entitlement, all issued credential records for that user and credential type are deleted. The wallet can no longer refresh the credential.
* *Credential update (revision change)* -- When an administrator updates the credential entitlement, the attribute snapshot is refreshed and the revision is incremented. This update does not invalidate existing refresh tokens. The wallet can continue to refresh the credential, and claims mapped from user attributes contain the current values. For details, see <<_oid4vci_attribute_snapshot,Understanding Attribute Snapshots and Credential Claims>>.

[WARNING]
====
Requesting an OID4VCI scope during login produces a refresh token whose lifetime is governed by the *Credential Lifetime* setting rather than the user session lifespan. Because this token remains valid after user logout, it must be stored securely within the wallet application.
====

[NOTE]
====
OID4VCI scope access tokens are purpose-locked exclusively to the {project_name} credential endpoint. Because their audience (`aud`) claim is set to the credential endpoint URL, they are blocked from accessing other {project_name} APIs, including the introspection, Admin REST, and Account REST APIs.
====

For details on configuring these settings, see <<_understanding_credential_lifetime_vs_refresh_interval, dedicated section>>.

==== Responding to Compromise

===== User Account Compromised

If a user account is compromised, follow these steps to revoke all issued credentials and prevent further issuance:

. *Disable the user account* -- Navigate to *Users* > select the user > toggle *Enabled* to *Off*. This prevents new logins.
. *Revoke active sessions* -- Navigate to *Users* > select the user > *Sessions* and click *Sign out all active sessions*. This sets the user's not-before policy and invalidates only that user's active tokens, including refresh tokens used for credential refresh.
+
.Session revocation
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-user-sessions-revocation.png[Sessions revocation page, width=650]
. *Revoke credential entitlements* -- Navigate to *Users* > select the user > *Verifiable Credentials* tab. Revoke each credential type entitlement. This deletes all issued credential records and prevents any future credential issuance for this user.

[NOTE]
====
Verifiable Credentials already held by wallets remain cryptographically valid until their `exp` claim expires. Setting a short *Credential Refresh Interval* (`vc.refresh_interval_in_seconds`) limits the window of exposure. For example, a 24-hour refresh interval means a compromised credential becomes unusable within 24 hours of the session revocation, since the wallet cannot refresh it.
====

===== Client or Wallet Application Compromised

If a client application or wallet is compromised, follow these steps to prevent further use of credentials issued through that client. Credentials already held by wallets remain valid until their `exp` claim expires:

. *Disable the client* -- Navigate to *Clients* > select the compromised client > toggle *Enabled* to *Off*. This prevents all token operations, including refresh, through this client.
+
.Disabling a compromised client
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-client-disable.png[Client settings page with Enabled toggle, width=650]
. All refreshes of existing credentials through this client become impossible.
. *Alternative*: Delete and re-create the client. Deleting a client automatically removes all issued credential records associated with it.

[NOTE]
====
There is currently no bulk API to revoke all credentials issued through a specific client. To revoke individual credentials, use the per-user Admin UI or REST API as described above. Each issued credential record shows the *Wallet Client* it was issued through, which helps identify affected credentials.
====

==== Self-Service Credential Management via the Account Console

In addition to administrator-managed credential operations, users can view and manage their own Verifiable Credentials through the {project_name} Account Console. This enables self-service workflows where users can monitor their issued credentials and revoke them if needed.

===== Prerequisites

The Account Console Verifiable Credentials page is available when all of the following conditions are met:

* The `oid4vc-vci` server feature is enabled.
* Verifiable Credentials are enabled at the realm level (in *Realm Settings*).
* The user has one of the following account roles:
** `manage-account` -- Grants full access, including viewing and revoking credentials.
** `view-verifiable-credentials` -- Grants read-only access to view credentials.
** `manage-verifiable-credentials` -- Grants access to view and revoke credentials.
* When using either Verifiable Credentials-specific role, add that role to the `account-console` client's scope mappings; these roles are not mapped there by default.

===== Viewing Credentials in the Account Console

Users can access their Verifiable Credentials by navigating to the *Verifiable Credentials* page in the Account Console sidebar.

.Verifiable Credentials page in the Account Console
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-account-vc-page.png[Verifiable Credentials page in the Account Console, width=750]

The page lists each credential type assigned to the user, showing the credential scope name, creation date, and last updated date. Each credential row provides the following actions:

* *View Issued Credentials* -- Opens a modal showing all individual issued credentials for this credential type, including issuance date, expiration date, and wallet client information.
+
.Issued credentials modal in the Account Console
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-account-issued-credentials-modal.png[Issued credentials modal showing individual credentials in the Account Console, width=750]

* *Issue to Wallet* -- Initiates a credential offer flow that allows the user to receive the credential in their wallet. For additional details about credential offer, see the <<_oid4vci_credential_offer_aia,dedicated documentation section>>.
* *Revoke* -- Revokes the credential type entitlement and deletes all issued credential records for that credential type. This action is only available to users with the `manage-account` or `manage-verifiable-credentials` role.

===== Revoking Credentials in the Account Console

Users with the appropriate role can revoke credentials at two levels:

* *Credential type entitlement* -- Click *Revoke* on the credential row in the main list. This removes the entitlement and deletes all issued credential records for that user and credential type.
* *Individual issued credential* -- Click *View Issued Credentials*, then click *Revoke* on the specific issued credential. This removes only that credential record from the database.

[NOTE]
====
The `view-verifiable-credentials` role provides read-only access. Users with this role can view their credentials and issued credential details but cannot revoke them. The *Revoke* action buttons are hidden for users without revocation permissions.
====

[[_oid4vci_proofs]]
=== Proof Types and Key Binding in OID4VCI

A credential proof in OID4VCI is a cryptographic proof-of-possession that a wallet sends to an issuer ({project_name}) to show it controls the private key meant to be
bound to the new credential.

Purposes of the proof are:

* **Anti-replay** - the nonce in the proof prevents a captured credential request from being replayed
* **Key binding** - the public proof key embedded in the VC ties the credential to the Wallet's key pair. When credential is later presented by the wallet to the
credential verifier, verifier is able to cryptographically verify issuer as well as holder/wallet. Verifying of the holder is possible in case that key binding was used.

[[_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases]]
==== Example use cases

===== Use Case 1: Credential request without proof

.Credential request without proof
image::images/oid4vci/proof_part1-no-proof.drawio.svg[Credential request without proof]

. Wallet sends credential request without a `proofs` parameter
. Issuer/{project_name} issues the credential but has no key to bind (for instance, in case of SD-JWT credential format, there is no `cnf` claim)
. Wallet creates the "verifiable credential presentation" and sends it to the verifier. However that presentation does not have key binding (for instance, in case of SD-JWT credential format, presentation ends with `~`)
. Verifier is able to verify issuer signature and eventually disclosed claims digests. However verifier cannot verify holder key binding and hence cannot distinguish the presenter from anyone else who stole the credential.
Risk is, that credential can be replayed or transferred to a different party.

===== Use Case 2: Credential request with non-attested proof

.Credential request with proof
image::images/oid4vci/proof_part2-jwt-proof.drawio.svg[Credential request with proof]

. Wallet fetches `c_nonce` from Issuer's nonce endpoint
. Wallet generates a key pair before credential request (if it does not have existing key pair already). Wallet signs `openid4vci-proof+jwt` (in case that `jwt` proof was used, which is most typical for this use case). JWT header carries public proof key inline (typically in `jwk` claim). The proofs is sent within credential request to the issuer ({project_name})
. Issuer validates proof JWT, extracts public key, embeds into the credential (for instance, in issued SD-JWT format, it is embedded into `cnf.jwk` claim)
. At presentation, Wallet appends a Key-Binding JWT signed with private proof key.
. Thanks to the key binding, verifier is able to verify Key-Binding JWT signature against `cnf.jwk` from issuer signed JWT. This allows to prevent bearer/replay attacks, which is main benefit against use case 1. For more details, see the <<_oid4vci_proofs_key_binding, Key Binding section>>

===== Use Case 3: Credential request with attested proof

Attestation is additional (optional) part of credential proof to add additional security. The purpose is to ensure that the proof key lives in a trusted environment (e.g. hardware secure element). It includes another entity called **Attester**. Attester is an external, trusted party. It participates in the creation of attested credential proofs for the credential wallets.
Attester has trust relationship with the issuer ({project_name}) as issuer should be able to verify attestation.

.Credential request with attested proof
image::images/oid4vci/proof_part3-attested-proof.drawio.svg[Credential request with attested proof]

. Wallet sends its public proof key to the Attester
. Attester checks the key is in a trusted environment (e.g. hardware-backed). Then issues key-attestation JWT signed by attestation private key
. Wallet either sends the key-attestation JWT as an `attestation` proof, or embeds it in the `key_attestation` header of a separate `jwt` proof.
. Issuer validates the attestation JWT against the Attester's public key (registered in Trusted Key IDP); for a `jwt` proof, it also validates the enclosing proof JWT. The public key (or certificate) of the Attester must be configured in {project_name} to establish trust.
. Issuer issues the credential including key-binding and returns to the wallet. It includes the wallet/holder key for the key binding (not the attestation key or attestation certificate)
. Same like step 4 for use case 2
. Same like step 5 for use case 2

The following sections document the proof types supported by OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance (OID4VCI), how to configure trusted attester keys, and how key binding works in the resulting credentials.

==== Supported Proof Types

{project_name} currently supports the following proof types for holder binding:

[cols="1,1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Proof Type
| Value
| Description

| JWT Proof
| `jwt`
| A signed JWT containing holder binding information. The key used to sign the JWT becomes the holder binding key in the credential. Supported for both <<_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases,use case 2 and use case 3>>.

| Attestation Proof
| `attestation`
| Proof containing key attestations from a trusted attestation authority. Supported for <<_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases,use case 3>>.
|===

When a credential requires cryptographic holder binding, the client must provide a proof of an appropriate type. The issuer validates the proof and extracts the binding key, which is then included in the issued credential.

[[_oid4vci_proofs_client_scope_config]]
==== Client Scope Configuration for Proof Types

To require key binding for a credential, configure the OID4VCI client scope with the appropriate attributes. These settings are advertised in the issuer metadata as `cryptographic_binding_methods_supported` and `proof_types_supported`, and they determine which proof types the wallet can use.

.Client scope configuration for proofs
image::images/oid4vci/proof_client_scope_config.png[Client scope configuration for proofs]

Most relevant options of the client scope related to proofs and key binding:

* **Cryptographic binding required** - When OFF, proofs are not required in credential request and key binding will not be used for verifiable credentials. This is <<_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases, use case 1 from examples above>>.
When this is ON, proofs are required in credential request and key binding will be used as specified in the <<_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases, use cases 2 and 3 from examples above>>.
If **Cryptographic binding required** is not enabled, the issuer metadata omits `cryptographic_binding_methods_supported` and `proof_types_supported`.

* **Supported proof types** - The attribute accepts a comma-separated list of supported proof types, currently `jwt` and `attestation`.

* **Cryptographic binding methods** - Comma separated list of key binding methods. Typical value is `jwk` for the supported credential formats like SD-JWT format, but might be different according to what particular format supports.

* **Key attestations required** - If ON, then proofs must be always attested as specified in the <<_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases, use case 3 above>>

* **Key storage resistance levels** and **User authentication resistance levels** - If this is configured, the corresponding values must be included in the attestation proofs. Those will be included in the OID4VCI credential metadata. Details about this are in the https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-credential-issuance-1_0.html#appendix-D.2[section D.2 of the OID4VCI specification].

NOTE: The `proof_signing_alg_values_supported` values in the metadata are automatically included in the issuer metadata based on the realm's supported asymmetric signing algorithms.

==== Configuring Trusted Attesters

This is needed to be configured for the <<_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases, use case 3 from examples above>>.
{project_name} supports JWT proofs that can optionally include key attestations, and the `attestation` proof type. To validate these attestations, configure the trusted attester keys through trust-material identity providers and link those identity providers to the OID4VCI client.

Trusted attester keys are configured per client because different wallets can rely on different attestation authorities. The former realm-level options **Trusted Key IDs** and **Trusted Keys (JSON)** are no longer used for OID4VCI proof validation.

===== Admin Console

. Create or configure a trust-material identity provider, such as **Default Trust**, that exposes the trusted attester public keys or X.509 trust anchors.
** For `kid`-based attestations, configure a JWKS URL or validating public key.
** For `x5c`-based attestations, enable **Use X.509 attestation trust**, provide a PEM bundle containing only self-signed device-vendor attestation CA roots, and configure **Required extended key usages** with the accepted Extended Key Usage (EKU) OIDs. When at least one OID is configured, the attestation end-entity certificate must contain an EKU extension with at least one OID that exactly matches a configured value; otherwise, validation fails. When the list is empty, no EKU restriction is applied and the trust anchors alone decide trust.
. Go to *Clients* and select the wallet client that requests credentials.
. Open the *Advanced* tab.
. In the *OpenID Verifiable Credentials* section, enable **Enable OID4VCI**.
. In **OID4VCI Attester Trust Identity Providers**, select the trust-material identity providers that contain the trusted attester public keys.
. Save the client.

OID4VCI does not define a universal EKU OID for key attestation. Use the OID specified by the device vendor or the applicable attestation trust framework. For example, a private test PKI could place `1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.1` in both the certificate and the configuration to demonstrate exact matching. The `32473` private enterprise number is reserved for documentation and must not be used in production.

WARNING: The built-in OIDC identity provider exposes only JWK trust material and cannot provide X.509 trust anchors for `x5c`-based attestations. Use **Default Trust**, or a custom trust-material identity provider that implements X.509 trust resolution, for `x5c`-based attestations.

WARNING: Certificate revocation checking is not currently supported for `x5c` key-attestation certificate chains. Before trusting an attestation CA, ensure that revoked attestation certificates are rejected by a mandatory revocation mechanism outside {project_name}.

The **OID4VCI Attester Trust Identity Providers** option is only shown when **Enable OID4VCI** is enabled for the client. It accepts only trust-material identity providers from the current realm. If no trust-material identity provider is configured, the dropdown has no values to select.

===== Client Attribute

[cols="1,1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Attribute
| Default
| Description

| `oid4vci.attester_trust_idps`
| none
| Comma-separated aliases of trust-material identity providers containing trusted attester public keys or X.509 attestation roots for OID4VCI key attestation validation.

|===

===== Admin REST API

Use the Admin REST API when you need to configure the client attribute directly.

[source,bash]
----
curl -X PUT "https://localhost:8443/admin/realms/{realm}/clients/{client-uuid}" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "attributes": {
          "oid4vci.enabled": "true",
          "oid4vci.attester_trust_idps": "alias-1,alias-2"
        }
      }'
----

For a JWT proof with a `key_attestation` JOSE header, or for an `attestation` proof, {project_name} resolves the attester signing key from the configured identity providers. Key resolution can use the attestation JWT header and payload, including the `kid`, `alg`, and `iss` values. If no configured identity provider trusts the key or certificate chain, proof validation fails.

===== X.509 Certificate-Chain Validation

For an `x5c`-based key attestation, the certificates presented in the attestation JWT and the trust material configured in the identity provider have different roles:

[source,text]
----
Attestation JWT JOSE header                   Default Trust identity provider
---------------------------                   -------------------------------
x5c[0]: attestation leaf certificate          Trusted certificates:
         - signs the attestation JWT            device-vendor root CA
         - must be an end-entity certificate    (self-signed trust anchor)
         - contains an allowed EKU

x5c[1..n]: intermediate CA certificates       Allowed attestation extended
           needed to build the path            key usages:
           (if any)                             device-vendor attestation EKU

x5c[last]: device-vendor root CA              The same root is configured
           (optional)                          as the trust anchor

                    Certificate path built by Keycloak
       attestation leaf -> intermediate CA(s) -> configured root CA
----

The first `x5c` entry must be the certificate containing the public key that signed the attestation JWT. Each following entry must be an issuer of the previous certificate. The entries are base64-encoded DER certificates, not PEM values or base64url-encoded values.

Include any intermediate CA certificates required to connect the leaf to the configured root. The root certificate can be the final `x5c` entry, but it is not required because the same root is already configured as a trust anchor. For example, if the configured root directly issued the leaf, `x5c` can contain only the leaf certificate.

For each selected X.509-capable trust-material identity provider, {project_name} independently builds a certificate path from the leaf to a root configured in that provider. The leaf must be an end-entity certificate, and its Extended Key Usage (EKU) extension must contain at least one OID allowed by the same provider. Trust roots and EKU policies from different providers are never combined.

A root included in `x5c` does not become trusted merely by being present. It must match a root configured in the identity provider. The JVM system truststore is never used as attestation trust.

Do not place public Web PKI roots or the general {project_name} TLS truststore in an attestation trust provider. Each provider should represent one device-vendor trust domain so its roots and certificate policy cannot be combined with another provider accidentally.

==== Creating and Sending JWT Proofs

JWT proofs are the most common proof type. They support the <<_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases, use cases 2 and 3 from examples above>>. The following steps describe creation of a JWT proof without attestation (use case 2):

===== 1. Obtain a Nonce

First, call the nonce endpoint to obtain a fresh nonce:

[source,bash]
----
curl -X POST "https://localhost:8443/realms/{realm}/protocol/oid4vc/nonce" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN"
----

Response:
[source,json]
----
{
  "c_nonce": "abc123def456...",
  "c_nonce_expires_in": 300
}
----

===== 2. Create the JWT Proof

The JWT proof must contain the following claims:

[cols="1,1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Claim
| Required
| Description

| `iss`
| Conditional
| For client-bound flows, must be the client_id. For anonymous flows, omit this claim.

| `aud`
| Yes
| Must be the Credential Issuer Identifier of the issuing realm

| `nonce`
| Yes
| The c_nonce value obtained from the nonce endpoint.

| `iat`
| Yes
| Issued-at time (Unix timestamp). Must be within 30 seconds of server time.

| `exp`
| No
| Expiration time. If provided, must be in the future.

| `nbf`
| No
| Not-before time. If provided, must be before server time + 10 seconds.
|===

.Header Requirements
[cols="1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Header
| Description

| `typ`
| Must be `openid4vci-proof+jwt`

| `alg`
| One of the algorithms listed in `proof_signing_alg_values_supported` (e.g., `ES256`, `RS256`, `PS256`)

| `jwk` or `kid` or `x5c`
| The binding key. Only one of these should be present.
|===

====== Example: JWT Proof with JWK in Header

[source,javascript]
----
// Header
{
  "typ": "openid4vci-proof+jwt",
  "alg": "ES256",
  "jwk": {
    "kty": "EC",
    "crv": "P-256",
    "x": "f83OJ3B2f4GuoXv...d83rVU",
    "y": "X_5R34qL2Y8ZdqU..."
  }
}

// Payload
{
  "iss": "your-client-id",
  "aud": "https://localhost:8443/realms/myrealm",
  "nonce": "abc123def456...",
  "iat": 1719785014
}
----

====== Example: JWT Proof with kid Header

[source,javascript]
----
// Header
{
  "typ": "openid4vci-proof+jwt",
  "alg": "ES256",
  "kid": "my-binding-key-id"
}

// Payload
{
  "iss": "your-client-id",
  "aud": "https://localhost:8443/realms/myrealm",
  "nonce": "abc123def456...",
  "iat": 1719785014
}
----

===== 3. Send the Credential Request

Include the JWT proof in the credential request:

[source,json]
----
{
  "format": "jwt_vc_json",
  "credential_configuration_id": "my-credential-config",
  "proofs": {
    "jwt": ["eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6Im9wZW5pZDh2Y2ktcHJvb2Yrand0IiwiandrIjp7Imt0eSI6IkVDIiwiY3J2IjoiUC0yNTYiLCJ4IjoiZjgzak8zQjJmNFdndU...=="]
  }
}
----

==== Using Attestation Proofs

Attestation proofs allow the holder to prove key ownership through an attestation authority. This is useful for hardware-backed keys or keys managed by secure enclaves.
The example is described in the <<_oid4vci_proofs_use_cases, use case 3 from examples above>>.

===== Structure of an Attestation Proof

An attestation proof is a JWT containing:

.Header
[cols="1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Header
| Description

| `typ`
| `openid4vci-attestation+jwt`

| `kid`
| Key ID of the attestation signing key

| `alg`
| Algorithm (e.g., `ES256`)
|===

.Payload
[cols="1,1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Claim
| Required
| Description

| `nonce`
| Yes
| The c_nonce from the nonce endpoint

| `iat`
| Yes
| Issued-at time

| `exp`
| Yes
| Expiration time

| `attested_keys`
| Yes
| Array of JWK objects representing the holder's attested keys

| `key_storage`
| No
| List of acceptable key storage attack potential levels (ISO 18045)

| `user_authentication`
| No
| List of acceptable user authentication attack potential levels

| `status`
| Yes
| Object with `status` claim (e.g., `{"status": "valid"}`)
|===

===== Credential Request with Attestation Proof

[source,json]
----
{
  "format": "jwt_vc_json",
  "credential_configuration_id": "my-credential-config",
  "proofs": {
    "attestation": ["eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6Im9wZW5pZDh2Y2ktYXR0ZXN0YXRpb24rand0Ii...=="]
  }
}
----

[[_oid4vci_proofs_key_binding]]
==== Key Binding in Credentials

The binding key from the proof is included in the issued credential to ensure the holder possesses the corresponding private key.

===== JWT VC JSON Format

For `jwt_vc_json` format credentials, the binding key is included in the `cnf` (confirmation) claim:

[source,json]
----
{
  "iss": "https://localhost:8443/realms/myrealm",
  "vc": {
    "@context": ["https://www.w3.org/2018/credentials/v1"],
    "type": ["VerifiableCredential", "MyCredential"],
    "credentialSubject": { ... },
    "cnf": {
      "jwk": {
        "kty": "EC",
        "crv": "P-256",
        "x": "f83OJ3B2f4GuoXv...d83rVU",
        "y": "X_5R34qL2Y8ZdqU..."
      }
    }
  },
  "iat": 1719785014,
  "exp": 1751321014,
  "jti": "unique-credential-id"
}
----

===== SD-JWT Format

For `dc+sd-jwt` format credentials, the binding key is included as a disclosure in the SD-JWT:

[source]
----
eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiJ9.eyJAY29udGV4dCI6WyJodHRwczovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAxOC9jcmVkZW50aWFscy92MSJdLCJ0eXBlIjpbIlZlcmlmaWFibGVDcmVkZW50aWFsIiwiTXlDcmVkZW50aWFsIl0sImNyZWRlbnRpYWxTdWJqZWN0Ijp7fSwiY25mIjp7Imp3ayI6eyJrdHkiOiJFQyIsImNydiI6IlAtMjU2IiwieCI6ImY4M09PM0IyZjRHZ3VYdi4uLmQ4M3JWVSJ9fX0.K3ZkVYZ2B9...#eyJjdHgiOnsidHlwZSI6ImNuZiIsIm9iaiI6eyJrdHkiOiJFQyIsImNydiI6IlAtMjU2In19"
----

The holder binding key appears in the `_sd_hash` of the SD-JWT, allowing verifiers to confirm the holder possesses the corresponding private key.

===== Verifying Key Binding

When presenting a credential, the verifier should:

1. Extract the `cnf` claim (for JWT VC) or verify the `_sd_hash` (for SD-JWT)
2. Challenge the holder to sign a challenge with the corresponding private key
3. Verify the signature matches the bound key

==== Complete Example: Credential Request with JWT Proof

[source,bash]
----
# 1. Get an access token (OAuth2 flow)
# ... (obtain access token with appropriate scopes)

# 2. Obtain nonce
NONCE_RESPONSE=$(curl -X POST "https://localhost:8443/realms/myrealm/protocol/oid4vc/nonce" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN")
C_NONCE=$(echo $NONCE_RESPONSE | jq -r '.c_nonce')

# 3. Create JWT proof (pseudocode - use your JWT library)
PROOF_HEADER='{ "typ":"openid4vci-proof+jwt", "alg":"ES256", "jwk":{ "kty":"EC", "crv":"P-256", "x":"...", "y":"..." } }'
PROOF_PAYLOAD="{ \"iss\":\"your-client-id\", \"aud\":\"https://localhost:8443/realms/myrealm\", \"nonce\":\"$C_NONCE\", \"iat\":$(date +%s) }"
JWT_PROOF=$(create_jwt "$PROOF_HEADER" "$PROOF_PAYLOAD" "$YOUR_PRIVATE_KEY")

# 4. Send credential request
curl -X POST "https://localhost:8443/realms/myrealm/protocol/oid4vc/credential" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "format": "jwt_vc_json",
    "credential_configuration_id": "my-credential-config",
    "proofs": {
      "jwt": ["'"$JWT_PROOF"'"]
    }
  }'
----

Additional working examples on how to setup and use proofs can be seen from the https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak-playground/blob/main/fapi-playground/README.md#oid4vci-demo[Keycloak playground repository] (not officially supported repository).

[[_oid4vci_credential_request]]
=== Requesting Credentials

This section explains how a wallet interacts with {project_name} to request and obtain a Verifiable Credential using the Authorization Code Flow.

==== 1. Discovering Issuer Metadata

Wallets often start from a credential offer, for example from a QR code or link. The credential offer contains the issuer identifier (`credential_issuer`), which the wallet uses to locate the Credential Issuer Metadata endpoint.

The wallet then discovers the issuer's capabilities by calling the Credential Issuer Metadata endpoint. This endpoint provides details about the credential formats supported, cryptographic binding methods, and the URLs of other necessary endpoints (such as the authorization, token, and credential endpoints).

[source,bash]
----
curl -s -X GET "https://localhost:8443/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer/realms/{realm}"
----

The JSON response contains the `credential_configurations_supported` object, which lists all available credentials and their configurations. From this metadata, the wallet determines the `credential_configuration_id` it wishes to request and identifies the `credential_endpoint` and `token_endpoint`.

[source,json]
----
{
  "credential_issuer": "https://localhost:8443/realms/{realm}",
  "credential_endpoint": "https://localhost:8443/realms/{realm}/protocol/oid4vc/credential",
  "batch_credential_endpoint": "https://localhost:8443/realms/{realm}/protocol/oid4vc/batch-credential",
  "nonce_endpoint": "https://localhost:8443/realms/{realm}/protocol/oid4vc/nonce",
  "authorization_servers": [
    "https://localhost:8443/realms/{realm}"
  ],
  "credential_configurations_supported": {
    "membership-credential": {
      "format": "jwt_vc_json",
      "scope": "membership-credential",
      "cryptographic_binding_methods_supported": [
        "jwk"
      ],
      "credential_signing_alg_values_supported": [
        "ES256",
        "RS256"
      ],
      "credential_definition": {
        "type": [
          "VerifiableCredential",
          "membership-credential"
        ]
      },
      "proof_types_supported": {
        "jwt": {
          "proof_signing_alg_values_supported": [
            "ES256"
          ]
        }
      },
      "credential_metadata": {
        "display": [
          {
            "name": "IdentityCredential",
            "locale": "en-US",
            "description": "Digitally verifiable identity credential",
            "background_color": "#12107c",
            "text_color": "#ffffff"
          }
        ],
        "claims": [
          {
            "path": [
              "credentialSubject",
              "given_name"
            ],
            "mandatory": true,
            "display": [
              {
                "name": "Given Name",
                "locale": "en-US"
              }
            ]
          },
          {
            "path": [
              "credentialSubject",
              "family_name"
            ],
            "mandatory": true,
            "display": [
              {
                "name": "Family Name",
                "locale": "en-US"
              }
            ]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }
}
----

==== 2. OIDC Authorization Request

To initiate the Authorization Code Flow, the wallet must direct the user to the {project_name} Authorization Endpoint. The wallet requests access to specific credentials using either standard OpenID Connect **Scopes** or the finer-grained **Authorization Details** parameter.

===== Using Scopes

If credentials are mapped directly to scopes, the wallet includes the scope advertised for the credential configuration in the `scope` parameter alongside `openid`. This scope is the name of the client scope and can be different from the `credential_configuration_id`.

[source,http]
----
GET /realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/auth
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=my-wallet-client
  &redirect_uri=http://localhost:8080/callback
  &scope=openid membership-credential
  &code_challenge=xyz...
  &code_challenge_method=S256
----

===== Using Authorization Details (Recommended)

Alternatively, the wallet can use the `authorization_details` parameter to request credentials. This is highly recommended for complex credential configurations. The `authorization_details` parameter is a JSON array that specifies the exact credential being requested.

[source,json]
----
[
  {
    "type": "openid_credential",
    "credential_configuration_id": "membership-credential"
  }
]
----

To pass this in the URL, the JSON array must be URL-encoded:

[source,http]
----
GET /realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/auth
  ?response_type=code
  &client_id=my-wallet-client
  &redirect_uri=http://localhost:8080/callback
  &scope=openid
  &authorization_details=%5B%7B%22type%22%3A%22openid_credential%22%2C%22credential_configuration_id%22%3A%22membership-credential%22%7D%5D
  &code_challenge=xyz...
  &code_challenge_method=S256
----

[TIP]
====
**Use Pushed Authorization Requests (PAR)**: The `authorization_details` parameter can quickly become large and exceed standard URL length limits. It is highly recommended to use the **PAR endpoint** (`/realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/ext/par/request`) to push the authorization payload via a back-channel `POST` request. The PAR endpoint returns a `request_uri`, which is then safely passed to the frontend authorization endpoint.
====

==== 3. OIDC Token Request

After the user successfully authenticates and grants consent, {project_name} redirects the user back to the wallet with an authorization code. The wallet exchanges this code for an Access Token at the Token Endpoint.

[source,bash]
----
curl -X POST "https://localhost:8443/realms/{realm}/protocol/openid-connect/token" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded" \
  -d "grant_type=authorization_code" \
  -d "code=AUTHORIZATION_CODE" \
  -d "client_id=my-wallet-client" \
  -d "client_secret=<YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET>" \
  -d "redirect_uri=http://localhost:8080/callback" \
  -d "code_verifier=PKCE_CODE_VERIFIER"
----

**Token Response and Credential Identifiers**

If the authorization request was successful, the token response includes the access token and the authorized `authorization_details`. Critically, {project_name} will populate the `credential_identifiers` array inside the authorization details. This identifier must be extracted, as it is required for the subsequent credential request.

[source,json]
----
{
  "access_token": "eyJhbGci...",
  "token_type": "Bearer",
  "expires_in": 300,
  "scope": "openid membership-credential",
  "authorization_details": [
    {
      "type": "openid_credential",
      "credential_configuration_id": "membership-credential",
      "credential_identifiers": [
        "membership-credential"
      ]
    }
  ]
}
----

==== 4. Requesting the Credential

With the Access Token and the `credential_identifier` in hand, the wallet can now request the credential.

First, the wallet must obtain a fresh challenge nonce from the `/protocol/oid4vc/nonce` endpoint, and use it to construct a cryptographic Proof of Possession (typically a JWT proof signed by the wallet's private key). See <<_oid4vci_proofs,Proof Types and Key Binding in OID4VCI>> for details about supported proof types and proof payloads.

Then, the wallet submits the request to the Credential Endpoint (`/protocol/oid4vc/credential`):

[source,bash]
----
curl -X POST "https://localhost:8443/realms/{realm}/protocol/oid4vc/credential" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "credential_identifier": "membership-credential",
    "proofs": {
      "jwt": [
        "eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5c...<base64url-encoded-jwt-proof>"
      ]
    }
  }'
----

[IMPORTANT]
====
If the Access Token contains `authorization_details`, the `credential_identifier` in the credential request **must exactly match** the identifier returned in the Token Response. If it does not match, the request will be rejected with an `unknown_credential_identifier` error.
====

{project_name} validates the access token, verifies the proof signature against the provided public key, checks user requirements (like mandatory claims), and returns the signed Verifiable Credential.

**Sample Credential Response (JWT VC)**

For a standard JWT VC (`jwt_vc_json` format), the response includes the signed credential string and a new nonce for any subsequent requests:

[source,json]
----
{
  "format": "jwt_vc_json",
  "credential": "eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIs...<base64url-encoded-jwt>",
  "c_nonce": "new_nonce_value_for_next_request",
  "c_nonce_expires_in": 86400
}
----

==== Requesting an SD-JWT Credential

Requesting an SD-JWT (Selective Disclosure JWT) credential follows the exact same process described above, but the target `credential_configuration_id` must map to a client scope configured for the `dc+sd-jwt` format.

When {project_name} processes the request, it issues a credential where claims are hidden behind cryptographic salts (disclosures). The issued SD-JWT credential response looks like this:

[source,json]
----
{
  "format": "dc+sd-jwt",
  "credential": "eyJhbGciOiJFUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6ImRjK3NkLWp3dCJ9.eyJfaXNzIjoi...~<disclosure_1>~<disclosure_2>~",
  "c_nonce": "new_nonce_value_for_next_request",
  "c_nonce_expires_in": 86400
}
----

The `credential` string is a concatenated format combining the Issuer-Signed JWT and the base64url-encoded Disclosures, separated by tildes (`~`). The holder binding key (from the wallet's proof) is embedded securely in the `_sd_hash` confirmation claim inside the SD-JWT.

[[_oid4vci]]
== Configuring {project_name} as a Verifiable Credential Issuer

[WARNING]
====
This feature is in preview and is not fully supported. It is disabled by default and can be enabled with `--features=oid4vc-vci`. Alternatively, users who explicitly want to enable the full preview feature set can use `--features=preview`. Backward compatibility is not guaranteed, and future updates may introduce breaking changes.
====

{project_name} supports the https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-credential-issuance-1_0.html[OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance (OpenID4VCI)] protocol, enabling it to act as a credential issuer in decentralized identity ecosystems. With this protocol, you can issue digitally signed Verifiable Credentials (VCs) that relying parties (verifiers) can independently verify without contacting {project_name}.

This chapter explains what Verifiable Credentials are, how the protocol works, and walks you through every step needed to configure {project_name} for credential issuance.

=== What are Verifiable Credentials?

Verifiable Credentials are the digital equivalent of physical credentials like passports, driver's licenses, or university degrees. They are cryptographically signed, tamper-evident data structures containing claims about an entity (a person, organization, or device).
The key properties of VCs:

- **Tamper-evident**: Any alteration invalidates the cryptographic signature.
- **Privacy-preserving**: Support selective disclosure (e.g., prove you are over 18 without revealing your exact birthdate).
- **Offline-verifiable**: A verifier can check the credential's validity without contacting the issuer.
- **Holder-controlled**: The individual receiving the credential controls when and with whom to share it.

==== Verifiable Credential Formats

OpenID4VCI supports multiple credential formats for encoding and issuing credentials:

- https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc-13.html[SD-JWT VC] – Selective Disclosure JSON Web Token Verifiable Credential
- https://github.com/decentralized-identity/jwt-vc-presentation-profile[JWT VC] – JSON Web Token Verifiable Credential
- https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html[mDL/mdoc] – Mobile driver's license / mobile document format

{project_name} currently supports both SD-JWT VC and JWT VC for issuance. mDL/mdoc format has just experimental support in {project_name} and should not be used in production environments. It is planned for a proper support in the future releases.

=== The Issuer-Holder-Verifier Model

Verifiable Credentials rely on a trust model built around three distinct roles:

.Triangle of Trust — The Issuer-Holder-Verifier Model
image::images/oid4vci/triangle-of-trust.dio.svg[Diagram showing the Issuer-Holder-Verifier model, width=650]

* **Issuer** — The entity (in this case, {project_name}) that signs and issues credentials. Governed by _OpenID4VCI_.
* **Holder** — The individual or wallet that receives, stores, and presents credentials.
* **Verifier** — The relying party that validates the credential's authenticity and integrity. Governed by _OpenID4VP_.

An important privacy property: the issuer and verifier never communicate directly. The holder controls what information to share and with whom. This means the issuer cannot track where, when, or how credentials are used.

=== Why Use OpenID4VCI

OpenID4VCI brings verifiable credential issuance into the OpenID Connect ecosystem your organization already uses. Key benefits:

* **Interoperability** — Built on top of OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, making it straightforward to integrate with existing identity infrastructure.
* **Privacy and security** — Supports selective disclosure, key-bound credentials, and offline verification.
* **Regulatory compliance** — Aligns with frameworks like eIDAS 2.0 and emerging digital identity regulations worldwide.
* **Developer efficiency** — Leverages {project_name}'s existing authentication, authorization, and token management capabilities.

=== Real-World Applications

Verifiable Credentials open the door to a wide range of practical use cases:

* Digital identity cards or driver's licenses issued by governments, where citizens reveal only what is needed (age, residency) for a given transaction.
* Verifiable diplomas and certificates issued by educational institutions, which employers can instantly verify without contacting the school.
* Employee badges issued as VCs for secure office access and remote authentication.
* Event tickets that are tamper-evident and verifiable offline.
* Membership credentials for professional associations, granting access to gated content or conference venues.

=== How Credential Issuance Works: Two Core Flows

OpenID4VCI defines two primary ways to issue credentials. Which one to use depends on whether the user needs to authenticate interactively.

==== Authorization Code Flow

The Authorization Code Flow is an interactive flow where the holder must authenticate and explicitly consent to credential issuance. It is ideal when you need user approval before issuing a credential.

This flow reuses {project_name}'s standard OpenID Connect authorization endpoint, so no additional endpoint is needed for the authorization step. The wallet communicates through a registered OIDC client that must have OID4VCI enabled and the appropriate credential client scope assigned.

**How it works:**

. The **User** wants a credential and initiates the process through their wallet.
. The **Wallet** sends an Authorization Request to {project_name}'s Authorization Endpoint (via the registered OIDC Client).
. {project_name} prompts the **User** to log in and grant consent.
. The **User** authenticates and approves the credential request.
. {project_name} returns an authorization code to the **Wallet**.
. The **Wallet** exchanges the code at the Token Endpoint for an access token.
. The **Wallet** requests the Verifiable Credential from the Credential Endpoint (`/protocol/oid4vc/credential`), presenting the access token.
. {project_name} validates the request, signs the credential, and returns it to the **Wallet**.

.Authorization Code Flow — Credential Issuance
image::images/oid4vci/authorization-code-flow.drawio.svg[Sequence diagram of the Authorization Code Flow, width=750]

This flow is best suited for scenarios where the user should be in control and give explicit permission for each credential issued.

[[_oid4vci_pre_authorized_code_flow]]
==== Pre-Authorized Code Flow

The Pre-Authorized Code Flow is a non-interactive flow. The issuer creates a pre-approved credential offer, and the wallet can claim the credential without real-time user authentication. This is useful for bulk issuance, offline-capable scenarios, or when the user has already been authenticated through other means.

Pre-authorized credential offers can be created through the {project_name} Admin Console, the Admin REST API, or programmatically through a dedicated endpoint (`/protocol/oid4vc/create-credential-offer`). The wallet communicates through a registered OIDC client that must have OID4VCI enabled.

**How it works:**

. An **Admin** creates a pre-authorized credential offer in {project_name} (via a registered OIDC Client).
. {project_name} returns a pre-authorized code and a credential offer URI.
. The **Admin** delivers the pre-authorized code to the **Wallet** (via QR code, link, or email).
. The **Wallet** exchanges the pre-authorized code at the Token Endpoint for an access token.
. The **Wallet** requests the Verifiable Credential from the Credential Endpoint, presenting the access token.
. {project_name} validates the request and returns the signed credential.

.Pre-Authorized Code Flow — Credential Issuance
image::images/oid4vci/pre-authorized-code-flow.drawio.svg[Sequence diagram of the Pre-Authorized Code Flow, width=700]

An optional transaction code (`tx_code`) can add a second layer of security. The `tx_code` must be communicated through a separate channel from the pre-authorized code itself.

=== Configuring Credential Issuance in Keycloak

In {project_name}, Verifiable Credentials are managed through *ClientScopes*, with each ClientScope representing a single Verifiable Credential type. To enable the issuance of a credential, the corresponding ClientScope must be assigned to an OpenID Connect client - ideally as *optional*.

During the OAuth2 authorization process, the credential-specific scope can be requested by including the ClientScope's name in the `scope` parameter of the authorization request. [[_oid4vci_key_management]]
==== Key Management Configuration

Credentials are signed with a realm signing key. For SD-JWT VCs, the selected key must also provide an X.509 certificate chain that satisfies the https://openid.net/specs/openid4vc-high-assurance-interoperability-profile-1_0-final.html#section-6.1.1[HAIP issuer key resolution requirements]:

* The first certificate must be the leaf certificate for the credential signing key.
* The leaf certificate must not be self-signed.
* Any intermediate certificates must follow the leaf certificate in chain order.
* The trust anchor must not be included in the `x5c` JOSE header. If the configured chain ends with a self-signed root certificate, {project_name} removes it when creating the SD-JWT VC. Any non-self-signed trust anchor must be omitted from the configured chain.

[IMPORTANT]
====
Do not use a generated realm key to sign SD-JWT VCs. A generated key either has no certificate or uses a self-signed certificate, so SD-JWT VC issuance fails. This restriction does not apply to JWT VCs.
====

Elliptic Curve cryptography with the P-256 curve and `ES256` algorithm is recommended for OpenID4VC. To configure a suitable signing key:

. Obtain a P-256 private key and a corresponding leaf certificate issued by a certificate authority. Include intermediate certificates when applicable. The example how to create valid ES256 key is in the https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak-playground/blob/main/fapi-playground/keystores/oid4vci-ssl-test/README-generate-keystore.md[Keycloak playground repository] (this is just for the development purposes and not officially supported).
. Store the private key and its certificate chain in a supported Java keystore. The private-key entry must contain the leaf certificate first, followed by any intermediate certificates. You may append a self-signed root certificate, but you must not append a non-self-signed certificate that is intended to be the trust anchor.
. In the Admin Console, go to *Realm Settings* > *Keys* > *Providers*.
. Add a *java-keystore* provider and configure the keystore path, type, passwords, and key alias.
. Set *Algorithm* to `ES256` and *Key use* to `sig`.
. Make the provider active and assign it sufficient priority to become the active `ES256` realm key. Alternatively, explicitly select this key as the *Signing Key ID* when configuring the credential client scope.

[NOTE]
====
The keystore may contain a self-signed root certificate so that {project_name} can load and validate the complete chain. {project_name} removes a trailing self-signed root certificate from the SD-JWT VC and signed issuer metadata `x5c` headers. It does not remove a non-self-signed trust anchor, which must therefore be omitted from the configured chain.

For details about the keystore location and provider fields, see <<realm_keys,Configuring realm keys>>.
====

===== Time Claim Correlation Mitigation

To reduce the risk of correlation across multiple issuances or presentations, you can normalize time-related claims. This is an opt-in privacy feature configured in the **Time Claim Correlation Mitigation** section:

.Time Claim Correlation Mitigation
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-time-claim-mitigation.png[Time Claim Correlation Mitigation settings, width=650]

[cols="1,1,1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Setting
| Realm Attribute
| Default
| Description

| Time Claims Strategy
| `oid4vci.time.claims.strategy`
| Off
| Strategy to apply to time claims. Supported values: `off` (no normalization), `randomize` (subtract a random offset), `round` (truncate to a time unit boundary).

| Randomize Window
| `oid4vci.time.randomize.window.seconds`
| `86400` (24 hours)
| When strategy is `randomize`, the system subtracts a random number of seconds between 0 and this value from the original timestamp.

| Round Unit
| `oid4vci.time.round.unit`
| `SECOND`
| When strategy is `round`, timestamps are truncated to the selected unit boundary (UTC). Supported values: `SECOND`, `MINUTE`, `HOUR`, `DAY`.
|===

How normalization is applied during issuance:

* For JWT-VC, the credential `issuanceDate` is normalized at issuance; the JWT `nbf` is derived from the normalized value. If a mapper sets a VC `expirationDate`, it is normalized and emitted as JWT `exp`.
* For SD-JWT VCs, time-related claims (`iat`, `nbf`, `exp`) are typically set using protocol mappers such as the Issued At Time Claim Mapper. Values are automatically normalized according to the realm strategy.

=== Create Client Scopes with Mappers

Client scopes define **which user attributes** are included in Verifiable Credentials (VCs) and therefore represent the Verifiable Credential configuration itself. Each credential type is configured as a dedicated client scope using the **OpenID for Verifiable Credentials** protocol.

A client scope uses **protocol mappers** to map specific user attributes to claims within the credential. These protocol mappers also expose the corresponding metadata that is published through the Credential Issuer Metadata Endpoint.

Many OID4VCI client scope attributes can be configured directly through the {project_name} Admin Console:

. Ensure **Include in OpenID Provider Metadata** is toggled **On** — when enabled, this client scope is included in the OpenID Provider Metadata and the credential configuration will be advertised in the Issuer Metadata Endpoint response.
