[[_understanding_credential_lifetime_vs_refresh_interval]]
===== Understanding Credential Lifetime vs. Refresh Interval

{project_name} provides separate time-based settings for verifiable credential validity:

* **Credential Lifetime** (`vc.expiry_in_seconds`) — Controls how long the credential record remains valid in the database and determines the refresh token expiration. Default: 1 year (31536000 seconds).

* **Credential Refresh Interval** (`vc.refresh_interval_in_seconds`) — Controls the `exp` (expiration) claim in the actual VC JWT returned to the wallet. Default: 7 days (604800 seconds), or the credential lifetime if shorter.

This separation enables a periodic refresh cycle:

. The wallet receives a VC with a 7-day expiration
. The wallet also receives a refresh token valid for 1 year
. After 7 days, the VC expires (wallet can verify this locally)
. The wallet uses the refresh token to obtain a new access token
. The wallet requests a new VC, which is valid for another 7 days
. This cycle continues until the refresh token expires (after 1 year)
. After 1 year, both the refresh token and the database record expire, requiring re-authentication

This design provides:

* **Enhanced security** — Regular credential rotation reduces the impact of credential theft
* **Privacy protection** — Fresh credentials with updated timestamps prevent long-term correlation
* **User convenience** — Automatic refresh without re-authentication for up to 1 year

[IMPORTANT]
====
The credential refresh interval must not exceed the credential lifetime. {project_name} validates this constraint when creating or updating credential scopes. If you set a credential lifetime shorter than 7 days without explicitly configuring the refresh interval, the refresh interval automatically adjusts to match the credential lifetime.
====

==== Adding Protocol Mappers

Protocol mappers map user attributes into specific claims within the credential and also expose the corresponding metadata displayed at the Credential Issuer Metadata Endpoint. This section explains how to configure protocol mappers through the Admin Console.

After creating a client scope with the `oid4vc` protocol, add protocol mappers as follows:

. In the {project_name} Admin Console, navigate to *Client Scopes* and select the created client scope (e.g., `membership-credential`).
. Click the *Mappers* tab.
. Click *Add mapper* and select *By configuration*.
. From the list of mapper types, select the desired mapper (see <<available-mapper-types,Available Mapper Types>> below).
. Provide a **Name** for the mapper and configure the required fields.
. Click *Save*.

[[available-mapper-types]]
The following mapper types are available for the `oid4vc` protocol:

.Available OID4VCI Mapper Types
image::images/oid4vci/screenshot-oid4vci-add-mapper-selection.png[Available OID4VCI mapper type in the Add mapper dialog, width=650]

===== Minimum Mapper Configuration for Issuance

At a minimum, a credential should include the user's core identity attributes. For example, to issue a membership credential carrying the user's given name, family name, and email, configure the following mappers:

[cols="1,1,1,2", options="header"]
|===
| Mapper Name
| Mapper Type
| Config
| Description

| `given_name-mapper`
| User Attribute Mapper
| `claim.name`: `given_name` +
`userAttribute`: `firstName` +
`vc.display`: `[{"name":"Given Name","locale":"en"}]`
| Maps the user's first name to the `given_name` claim in the credential.

| `family_name-mapper`
| User Attribute Mapper
| `claim.name`: `family_name` +
`userAttribute`: `lastName` +
`vc.display`: `[{"name":"Family Name","locale":"en"}]`
| Maps the user's last name to the `family_name` claim.

| `email-mapper`
| User Attribute Mapper
| `claim.name`: `email` +
`userAttribute`: `email` +
`vc.display`: `[{"name":"Email","locale":"en"}]`

| `iat-mapper`
| Issued At Time Claim Mapper
| `claim.name`: `iat` +
`truncateToTimeUnit`: `HOURS` +
`valueSource`: `COMPUTE`

|===

[NOTE]
====
The `vc.display` property provides display metadata that wallets use to show human-readable descriptions for each claim. For time-based mappers like `iat`, display configuration is typically not required.

=== Create and Configure the Client

Set up a client to handle Verifiable Credential (VC) requests and assign the necessary scopes.
The client does not differ from regular OpenID Connect clients — with one exception: it must have the appropriate **optional ClientScopes** assigned that define the Verifiable Credentials it is allowed to issue.

After creating the client, you must configure its OID4VCI-specific settings.

==== Enabling OID4VCI for the Client

To allow a client to issue Verifiable Credentials, you must enable OID4VCI for that specific client:

. In the {project_name} Admin Console, navigate to *Clients* and select your client.
. Go to the *Advanced* tab.
. Scroll down to the **OpenID for Verifiable Credentials** section.
. Toggle **OID4VCI enabled** to **On**.
. Click *Save*.

image::images/oid4vci/enable-oid4vci-for-client.png[Enabling OID4VCI for the client, width=650]

==== Assigning Credential Scopes

For a client to issue a specific type of credential, the corresponding OID4VCI client scope (which defines the credential format and claims) must be assigned to it:

. In the {project_name} Admin Console, navigate to *Clients* and select your client.
. Go to the *Client scopes* tab.
. Click *Add client scope*.
. Select the credential scope you created earlier (e.g., `membership-credential`).
. Choose **Optional** as the assignment type (recommended for credential scopes).

This ensures that the client can request and process the scope during the authorization flow, allowing the wallet to receive the corresponding Verifiable Credential.

==== Creating a Client via the REST API

Alternatively, you can create and configure the client programmatically. Ensure the `oid4vci.enabled` attribute is set to `true` and the required client scope is added to `optionalClientScopes`.

. Create a JSON file (e.g., `my-wallet-client.json`) with the following content:
+
[source,json]
----
{
  "clientId": "my-wallet-client",
  "enabled": true,
  "protocol": "openid-connect",
  "publicClient": false,
  "serviceAccountsEnabled": true,
  "clientAuthenticatorType": "client-secret",
  "redirectUris": ["http://localhost:8080/*"],
  "directAccessGrantsEnabled": true,
  "defaultClientScopes": ["profile"],
  "optionalClientScopes": ["membership-credential"],
  "attributes": {
    "oid4vci.enabled": "true",
    "client.secret.creation.time": "1719785014",
    "client.introspection.response.allow.jwt.claim.enabled": "false",
    "login_theme": "keycloak",
    "post.logout.redirect.uris": "http://localhost:8080"
  }
}
----
+
- **clientId**: Unique identifier for the client.
- **optionalClientScopes**: Links the credential scope (e.g., `membership-credential`) for VC requests.
- **attributes.oid4vci.enabled**: Must be `true` to enable OID4VCI functionality for this client.

. Import the client using the following `curl` command:
+
[source,bash]
----
curl -k -X POST "https://localhost:8443/admin/realms/oid4vc-vci/clients" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @my-wallet-client.json
----

=== Verifying the Configuration

Validate the setup by accessing the **issuer metadata endpoint**:

. Open a browser or use a tool like `curl` to visit:
+
[source,bash]
----
https://localhost:8443/.well-known/openid-credential-issuer/realms/oid4vc-vci
----
+
A successful response returns a JSON object containing details such as:
- **Supported claims**
- **Credential formats**
- **Issuer metadata**

=== Conclusion

You have successfully configured **{project_name} as a Verifiable Credential Issuer** using the **OID4VCI protocol**.
This setup leverages {project_name}'s robust **identity management capabilities** to issue secure, **standards-compliant VCs**.

For a **complete reference implementation**, see the sample project:
https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak-oauth-sig/tree/main/oid4vci-deployment[OID4VCI deployment].

===== Exposing Local {project_name} to the Wallet

For local testing, {project_name} can run on the development machine as described in the previous OID4VCI setup sections. Because the wallet runs on a phone and needs an HTTPS issuer URL, expose the local {project_name} endpoint through an HTTPS tunnel, for example with `ngrok` or a similar tool.

If {project_name} listens locally with HTTPS on port `8443`, start the tunnel for that port:

Use the public HTTPS tunnel hostname consistently for the credential offer and the issuer metadata seen by the wallet. The wallet must see credential offers, issuer metadata, authorization endpoints, token endpoints, and credential endpoints under the same public HTTPS hostname.

[IMPORTANT]
====
The credential offer must target the same client id that the wallet uses during the OAuth flow. If the wallet sends a pushed authorization request with a client id that is not registered in the realm, {project_name} rejects the request with `client_not_found`.
====

===== Create a Credential Offer for Valera Wallet

[NOTE]
====
Instead of REST credential-offer, it is recommended to use AIA for creating credential offer. That is easier and does not need feature `oid4vc-vci-rest-credential-offer` to be enabled.
Follow <<_oid4vci_lissi_wallet_authz_code_flow,Lissi wallet Authorization code section>> or <<_oid4vci_lissi_wallet_preauthz_flow,Lissi wallet Pre-authorized code section>> for the details.
====

The examples in the flow sections below use the REST credential-offer endpoint. The bearer token must be issued to the Valera client for the user who creates the offer. When creating an offer for a different target user, that issuing user must have permission to create credential offers.

For the Authorization Code Flow test, create an offer for the `IdentityCredential` credential configuration and request a response that includes a QR code:

[source,bash]
----
ISSUER_BASE="https://your-tunnel-host.example/realms/{realm}"
ACCESS_TOKEN="<access-token-issued-to-the-Valera-client>"

curl -G "$ISSUER_BASE/protocol/oid4vc/create-credential-offer" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  --data-urlencode "credential_configuration_id=IdentityCredential" \
  --data-urlencode "pre_authorized=false" \
  --data-urlencode "type=uri_qr"
----

For the Pre-Authorized Code Flow test, create a pre-authorized offer for the user who owns the credential:

[source,bash]
----
ISSUER_BASE="https://your-tunnel-host.example/realms/{realm}"
ACCESS_TOKEN="<access-token-issued-to-the-Valera-client>"
TARGET_USER="<username>"

curl -G "$ISSUER_BASE/protocol/oid4vc/create-credential-offer" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  --data-urlencode "credential_configuration_id=IdentityCredential" \
  --data-urlencode "pre_authorized=true" \
  --data-urlencode "target_user=$TARGET_USER" \
  --data-urlencode "type=uri_qr"
----

The JSON response contains an `issuer`, a `nonce`, and a `qr_code` data URL. Display the `qr_code` value as an image for the wallet to scan, or use the returned issuer and nonce with your offer display component to create a deep link.

===== Authorization Code Flow Test

Use this flow when the holder should authenticate with {project_name} and approve issuance interactively.

. Ensure that the user has an available `IdentityCredential` credential in {project_name}.
. If you generate the offer through the REST credential-offer endpoint, the dedicated experimental `oid4vc-vci-rest-credential-offer` feature must also be enabled.
. Generate a credential offer for the Valera client without `pre_authorized=true`. The offer contains an `authorization_code` grant and an `issuer_state` value.
. Display the credential offer as a QR code or deep link and follow the <<_oid4vci_valera_wallet_claim_credential,Valera Wallet claiming steps>>.
. Valera starts the Authorization Code Flow. During this test, Valera used PAR and then redirected the user to {project_name} for authentication.
. Authenticate the user in {project_name} and approve the issuance flow.
. Valera exchanges the authorization code for a token and receives `authorization_details` containing `credential_identifiers`.
. Valera requests the credential from the credential endpoint with `credential_identifier` set to `IdentityCredential` and a JWT proof.
. {project_name} returns the issued `IdentityCredential` to the wallet.

The test succeeded with Valera Wallet 5.8.0. The final credential request used the credential identifier returned by {project_name}:

[source,json]
----
{
  "credential_identifier": "IdentityCredential",
  "proofs": {
    "jwt": ["<jwt-proof>"]
  }
}
----

===== Pre-Authorized Code Flow Test

Use this flow when the user has already been authenticated by the issuer and the wallet can redeem a pre-authorized credential offer without starting an interactive login flow on the phone.

This flow requires the dedicated experimental `oid4vc-vci-preauth-code` feature in addition to OID4VCI. Generating the offer with the `pre_authorized` and target user parameters in the following steps also requires the experimental `oid4vc-vci-rest-credential-offer` feature.

. Ensure that the user has an available `IdentityCredential` credential in {project_name}.
. Generate a credential offer for the Valera client with `pre_authorized=true` and the target user set to the user who owns the credential.
. Display the credential offer as a QR code or deep link and follow the <<_oid4vci_valera_wallet_claim_credential,Valera Wallet claiming steps>>.
. Valera exchanges the `pre-authorized_code` for an access token.
. Valera receives `authorization_details` containing `credential_identifiers`.
. Valera requests the credential from the credential endpoint with `credential_identifier` set to `IdentityCredential` and a JWT proof.
. {project_name} returns the issued `IdentityCredential` to the wallet.

The test succeeded with Valera Wallet 5.8.0. Earlier testing with Valera Wallet 5.7.6 failed because the JWT proof issuer claim did not match the client id used for the token request. This was no longer reproducible with the tested 5.8.0 version.

| Flow
| Result

| Authorization Code Flow
| Success
| Valera completed PAR, user authentication, token exchange, and the final credential request with `credential_identifier` set to `IdentityCredential`.

| Pre-Authorized Code Flow
| Success
| Valera exchanged the pre-authorized code and requested the credential with `credential_identifier` set to `IdentityCredential`.

[[_oid4vci_valera_troubleshooting]]
===== Troubleshooting

* In case of troubles, it can be good to enable user events as mentioned in the <<auditing-user-events,User events section>> and check the admin console events as well as server.log if there are any interesting details
* If {project_name} logs `client_not_found` during PAR, verify that the Valera client id `+https://wallet.a-sit.at/app+` exists in the realm.
* If {project_name} logs `invalid_redirect_uri`, verify that the Valera callback `asitplus-wallet://wallet.a-sit.plus/app/callback/provisioning` is listed as a valid redirect URI for the Valera client.
* If the final credential request fails with an `invalid_credential_request` about credential identifiers, verify that the wallet requests the credential with the `credential_identifier` returned in the token response `authorization_details`.

[id="authenticating-members_{context}"]

=  Authenticating members
[role="_abstract"]
When you enable organizations for a realm, user authentication is changed. If the user is recognized to be
authenticating in the context of an organization, the authentication flow changes on a per-organization basis.

When a realm is created, the authentication flows are automatically updated to enable specific steps to authenticate and onboard organization members. The authentication flows updated are:

* *browser*

* *first broker login*

The main change to the *browser* flow is that it defaults to an identity-first login so that users are identified before prompting for their credentials.
Concerning the first broker login flow, the main change is the ability to automatically add users as organization members once they authenticate through an identity provider associated with an organization and successfully complete the flow. Whether a user is actually added depends on the per-association configuration of the identity provider link -- specifically the auto-membership and membership type settings (see <<_managing_identity_provider_,Managing identity providers>>) -- and the domain gate, which checks that the user's email domain is claimed by the organization.

The choice to use an identity-first login or not depends on the existence of an organization in a realm.
If no organizations exist, the user follows the usual steps to authenticate using the username and password,
or any other step configured in the browser flow. Otherwise, the user is asked first for a username or email to continue authenticating to a realm.

The identity-first login main goal is to identify the user:

* Is the user an existing or a new user?
* Is the user a member of any organization within a realm?
* If an organization member, is the user linked to any identity provider associated with the organization?

Depending on the outcome when identifying the user, the authentication flow changes to either proceed with authentication
by asking for the user's credentials or eventually redirect the user automatically to authenticate within the organization security
boundaries through an identity provider.

== Understanding the identity-first login

In addition to identifying the user once the username is provided, the identity-first login is also responsible for:

* Matching an email domain to an organization.
* Deciding if the authentication flow should continue or not if an account already exists for the username provided
* Deciding how the user should be authenticated depending on how the domains and the identity providers are configured to an organization
and the set of credentials configured to the user account.
* Seamlessly authenticating users through an identity provider when the user's email domain matches a domain configured with identity provider routing and auto-redirect enabled.

The identity-first login provides the same capabilities that are provided by the usual login page with the username and
password fields. Users can still self-register by clicking the register link or choose any identity or social
broker that is not linked to an organization in that realm.

.Identity-first login page
image:images/organizations-identity-first-login.png[alt="Identity-first login page"]

In the case of a user that does not exist, if that user tries to authenticate using an email domain that matches an organization domain,
the identity-first login page appears again with a message that the username provided is not valid.
At this point, no need exists to ask the user for credentials.

.Identity-first when user does not exist
image:images/organizations-identity-first-error.png[alt="Identity-first login error"]

Several options exist to register the user allowing that user to authenticate to the realm and join an organization.

If the realm has the self-registration setting enabled, the user can click the *Register* link at the identity-first login page
and create an account at the realm.
After that, the administrator can send an invitation link to the user or manually add the user as a member of an organization.
For more details, see <<_managing_members_,Managing members>>.

If the organization has an identity provider without a domain and the *Hide on login page* setting is *OFF*, users can also click
the identity provider link at the identity-first login page to automatically create an account and join an organization
once they authenticate through the identity provider.
For more details, see <<_managing_identity_provider_,Managing identity providers>>.

In a similar situation to the previous section, the organization may have a domain configured to route to an identity provider
with auto-redirect enabled.
In this situation, the user is redirected to the identity provider if that user's email matches the domain.
Once the flow completes, an account is created and the user joins the organization. In case the user has any first-factor credentials
configured (e.g.: password, passwordless, kerberos) to the account, the user is not automatically redirected to the identity provider but asked to authenticate using their
credentials.

== How organization membership is determined during broker login

When a user authenticates through an identity provider that is linked to one or more organizations, the system determines
whether the user should be added as a member of an organization. This process involves several checks that run as part of
the first broker login flow.

=== Step 1: Invitation check

If the user is following an invitation link, the invitation determines which organization the user joins. The user is
added as an unmanaged member of the invited organization regardless of any identity provider link settings or domain
configuration. No further checks are performed.

=== Step 2: Organization resolution

The system determines which organization is the target of this login:

. *Auth session note*: If the identity-first login resolved an organization from the user's email domain, that organization is used.
. *Email domain match*: The user's email domain is matched against domains owned by organizations linked to this identity provider. Since each domain belongs to exactly one organization, this always identifies a single organization.
. *Single organization fallback*: If only one organization is linked to this identity provider, it is selected automatically.
. *No match*: If no organization can be determined, no membership is added.

=== Step 3: Resolved-organization gate

If organization resolution identified a specific organization, only that organization is evaluated for membership.
This prevents membership in other organizations when the user's login was initiated through a specific organization's domain.

If no organization was resolved (for example, during an IdP-initiated login via `kc_idp_hint`), all organizations
linked to the identity provider are evaluated.

=== Step 4: Per-association and domain gate checks

For each candidate organization:

. *Auto membership disabled*: If the identity provider link has auto membership set to disabled for this organization, the organization is skipped.
. *Auto membership enabled*:
* If the organization has no domains (domain-less organization), the domain gate is skipped and the user is added. This is useful for organizations that are domain-agnostic.
* If the organization has domains, the user's email domain must match at least one domain owned by the organization. If there is no match, the organization is skipped.

=== Step 5: Member assignment

If all checks pass:

* If the user is already a member of the organization, they are not re-added and their membership type is not changed.
* If the user is new to the organization, they are added with the membership type configured on the identity provider link (managed or unmanaged).

=== Login flow variations

SP-initiated login (email entered on login page)::
The identity-first login resolves a specific organization from the user's email domain. The resolved-organization gate
limits membership evaluation to that single organization. This is the most common flow.

IdP-initiated login (`kc_idp_hint`, no email entered)::
No organization is pre-resolved. The post-broker membership step evaluates all organizations linked to the identity provider.
The domain gate still prevents cross-organization membership -- users are only added to organizations whose domains match their email.

Invitation flow::
The invitation bypasses the entire auto-membership algorithm. The user is added to the invited organization as an
unmanaged member, regardless of identity provider link settings or domain configuration.

== Configuring existing authentication flows

As previously mentioned for new realms, authentication flows are automatically updated with the necessary steps
to support organizations and authenticate their members. For existing realms, in addition to enabling organizations to the
realm, you also need to manually update your existing (custom) authenticating flows.

Change the *browser* flow by following these steps:

.Procedure
. Duplicate the current flow bound to the *Browser flow* binding type to avoid breaking the flow you are currently using
. Click *Add sub-flow* and give it a name such as *My Organization*
. Move the newly added *My Organization* sub-flow to execute right after the *Identity Provider Redirector* execution step.
The main point here is that the sub-flow should happen before any other sub-flow or execution step that authenticates the
user using whatever credentials you support in your realm. Once added, change the *Requirement* to *Alternative*.
. Click *Add sub-flow* in the *My Organization* sub-flow and give it a name such as *My Organization - Conditional*. Once added, change the *Requirement* to *Conditional*.
. Click *Add condition* in the *My Organization - Conditional* sub-flow and select *Condition - user configured*. Once added, change the *Requirement* to *Required*.
. Click *Add step* in the *My Organization - Conditional* sub-flow and select the *Organization Identity-First Login
* execution step. Once added, change the *Requirement* to *Alternative*.
. Bind the authentication flow to the *Browser* binding type.

.Organizations browser flow
image:images/organizations-browser-flow.png[alt="Organizations browser flow"]

Once you enable the <<_enabling_organization_,Organizations>> setting to the realm and create
at least a single organization, you should be able to see the identity-first login page and start using organizations
in your realm.

Change the *first broker login* flow by following these steps:

.Procedure
. Duplicate the current flow bound to the *First broker login flow* bind type to avoid breaking the flow you are currently using
. Click *Add sub-flow* and give it a name such as `Organization Member - Conditional`. Once added, change the *Requirement* to *Conditional*.
. Click *Add condition* in the *Organization Member - Conditional* sub-flow and select *Condition - user configured*. Once added, change the *Requirement* to *Required*.
. Click *Add step* in the *Organization Member - Conditional* sub-flow and select the *Organization Member Onboard* execution step. Once added, change the *Requirement* to *Required*.
. Bind the authentication flow to the *First broker login* binding type.

.Organizations first broker flow
image:images/organizations-first-broker-flow.png[alt="Organizations first broker flow"]

You should now be able to authenticate using any identity provider associated with an organization
and have the user joining the organization as a member as soon as they complete the first browser login flow.

== Configuring how users authenticate

If the flow supports organizations, you can configure some of the steps to change how users authenticate to the realm.

For example, some use cases will require users to authenticate to a realm only if they are a member of any or a specific organization in the realm.

To enable this behavior, you need to enable the `Requires user membership` setting on the `Organization Identity-First Login` execution step by clicking on its settings.

If enabled, and after the user provides the username or email in the identity-first login page, the server will
try to resolve a organization where the user is a member by looking at any existing membership or based on the semantics of the <<_mapping_organization_claims_,organization>> scope,
if requested by the client. If not a member of an organization, an error page will be shown.

[id="common-organization-setup-recipes_{context}"]

= Common setup recipes

This section provides step-by-step instructions for common organization configurations. Each recipe shows how to
achieve a specific outcome using identity provider links, domain routing, and auto-membership settings.

For the full details on the settings referenced in these recipes, see <<_managing_identity_provider_,Managing identity providers>>,
<<managing-organization-domains_{context},Managing organization domains>>, and <<authenticating-members_{context},Authenticating members>>.

== Single identity provider with automatic managed membership

*Goal:* Users from a known email domain authenticate through the organization's identity provider and are automatically added as managed members.

*Prerequisites:* An identity provider created at the realm level.

.Procedure

. Create an organization with a domain (for example, `acme.com`).
. Go to the organization's *Identity providers* tab and click *Link identity provider*.
. Select the identity provider, set *Auto membership* to *ON* and *Membership type* to *Managed*. Click *Save*.
. Go to the organization's *Domains* tab and click the domain (`acme.com`).
. Select the linked identity provider from the dropdown and enable *Auto redirect*. Click *Save*.

*Result:* When a user enters an email like `alice@acme.com` on the login page, they are automatically redirected to the identity provider. After authenticating, they are added to the organization as a managed member. If the organization or the membership is removed, the user's account is also removed from the realm.

== Multiple domains with different identity providers

*Goal:* A single organization authenticates users from different email domains through different identity providers, with different membership types.

*Prerequisites:* Two identity providers created at the realm level (for example, `idp-corporate` and `idp-partner`).

.Procedure

. Create an organization with two domains (for example, `acme.com` and `partner.com`).
. Go to the organization's *Identity providers* tab:
.. Link `idp-corporate` with *Auto membership* ON and *Membership type* set to *Managed*.
.. Link `idp-partner` with *Auto membership* ON and *Membership type* set to *Unmanaged*.
. Go to the organization's *Domains* tab:
.. Edit `acme.com`: select `idp-corporate`, enable *Auto redirect*.
.. Edit `partner.com`: select `idp-partner`, enable *Auto redirect*.

*Result:* Users with `@acme.com` emails are routed to `idp-corporate` and added as managed members. Users with `@partner.com` emails are routed to `idp-partner` and added as unmanaged members. The organization controls the membership type independently for each identity provider link.

== Shared identity provider across multiple organizations

*Goal:* A single corporate identity provider (for example, a central EntraId instance) serves multiple organizations, with each organization only accepting users from its own email domain.

*Prerequisites:* One identity provider created at the realm level.

.Procedure

. Create Org-A with domain `acme.com`.
. Create Org-B with domain `globex.com`.
. In Org-A's *Identity providers* tab: link the identity provider with *Auto membership* ON and the desired *Membership type*.
. In Org-A's *Domains* tab: edit `acme.com`, select the identity provider, enable *Auto redirect*.
. In Org-B's *Identity providers* tab: link the same identity provider with *Auto membership* ON and the desired *Membership type*.
. In Org-B's *Domains* tab: edit `globex.com`, select the identity provider, enable *Auto redirect*.

*Result:* Both organizations share the same identity provider. The domain gate ensures that users with `@acme.com` are only added to Org-A, and users with `@globex.com` are only added to Org-B. A user whose email domain does not match either organization is not added to any organization.

NOTE: You can verify the shared configuration from the identity provider's realm-level detail page. The *Organizations* tab shows both organizations with their per-association settings, and the *Domains* sub-tab shows all domains routing to this provider.

NOTE: At most one organization can set the membership type to *Managed* for a given identity provider. If Org-A uses *Managed*, Org-B must use *Unmanaged*.

== Domain-less organization with auto-membership

*Goal:* An organization without domains automatically accepts any user who authenticates through a linked identity provider, regardless of their email domain.

*Prerequisites:* An identity provider created at the realm level.

.Procedure

. Create an organization without any domains.
. Go to the organization's *Identity providers* tab and link the identity provider with *Auto membership* ON.

*Result:* Any user authenticating through this identity provider is added to the organization because the domain gate is skipped for organizations without domains.

IMPORTANT: When the identity provider is also linked to other organizations, the resolved-organization gate applies. If a user's login was initiated through another organization's domain (SP-initiated), the domain-less organization is skipped. The domain-less organization only receives members when it is the resolved organization (for example, via the `organization:alias` scope) or when no organization was resolved (for example, during IdP-initiated login via `kc_idp_hint`).

== Identity provider linked without auto-membership

*Goal:* Link an identity provider to an organization for login convenience without automatically adding users as members. Membership is managed through invitations or manual admin actions only.

*Prerequisites:* An identity provider created at the realm level.

.Procedure

. Go to the organization's *Identity providers* tab and link the identity provider.
. Set *Auto membership* to *OFF*. The *Membership type* will be set to *Unmanaged* (managed is not available when auto membership is disabled).
. Click *Save*.

*Result:* The identity provider is available on the login page (unless hidden), and users can authenticate through it. However, users are not automatically added as organization members. To add users to the organization, use invitations or add them manually as realm users.

== Adding members through invitations

*Goal:* Invite a user to join an organization, regardless of identity provider or domain configuration.

*Prerequisites:* An organization exists.

.Procedure

. Go to the organization's *Members* tab and click *Add member*.
. Click *Invite member*.
. Provide the user's email address and optionally a first and last name.
. Click *Send*.

*Result:* The invited user receives an email with a link. When they click the link and authenticate (using any method, including an organization's identity provider), they are added to the organization as an unmanaged member. The invitation flow bypasses all auto-membership and domain gate logic -- the invitation determines the target organization directly.

NOTE: For more details on managing invitations, see <<_managing_members_,Managing members>>.
